utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I had gone back to try and shut the trucks off. The mortar rounds penetrated the tanks, and when the pump is running with no water in it the pump can burn-out. So I tried to get back to the truck to shut the trucks off but more rounds landed, several in close proximity. I got my bell wrung and some minor shrapnel because it landed close to me but fortunately a few feet above me. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, you're describing the event in some detail; whereas, the question was whether it was the only time you were actually physically wounded. I take it that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the only time metal got to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. And may I invite you to focus very much on what is specifically asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, on this occasion that we're talking about, in paragraph 23, would you agree that your conclusion was that you had been -- that the side that had shot at you with the mortar was the side controlled by Mr. Izetbegovic's forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: On that occasion, I thought that was the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon the placement of the craters from the mortar rounds, as well as the high angle of the same, and any other factors, did you come to the conclusion that you had been intentionally targeted by the forces of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I think somebody shot at us that day, and I think they came from behind us. Whether it was intentional or not, you know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Am I correct, sir, that apart from these three incidents, that is to say, the two incidents you discussed in direct and this incident you've now discussed with me, that there were many other occasions when either you or your colleagues were shot at by someone from either side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. We were shot at on a fairly regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to show you what's been marked as 1D00183. And, sir, while we wait for that, I could perhaps give you an introduction. This is a document that I obtained about another individual in a similar line of work from Rhode Island, Mr. Curt Varone, who we see from here is the director -- was the director of fire service division of legal and liability risk management institute, a practicing attorney in Rhode Island and Maine, with 37 years in the fire service, retiring in 2008 as deputy assistant chief of the Providence Fire Department, and director of public fire protection at the National Fire Protection Association. And if we move down, we see that he has two degrees, one in biology, one in fire safety, and in 1997 he completed the executive fire officer programme at the National Fire Academy, becoming the first person ever to receive four outstanding applied research awards. I don't suppose, sir, that you -- that Mr. Varone is someone that you would be familiar with through your line of work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No, that's a very senior fire-fighter there, and he would have been way out of my league.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I appreciate your candor. Now with respect to these institutions named herein, especially the National Fire Academy and the National Fire Protection Association, are these organisations ones that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just objection, relevance. What's the relevance of all this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We only are at the point where a person is identified. I take it that there will be some follow up and not just to make the Court familiar with the existence of Mr. Curt Varone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There will be some follow-up, Your Honours. I did this in this way so that both the witness and Your Honours could see the foundation for my questions, and I will be presenting a piece authored by Mr. Varone precisely on the topic of fire-fighters who are armed and what additional risks that brings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll listen to what comes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can repeat my question for you. The institutions mentioned herein, namely the National Fire Academy and the National Fire Protection Association, are those fire-fighting associations that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any affiliations with either of these institutions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I am sure that during the 1992 to 1995 time-period, I probably met the directors of both of them at various functions in the United States, the Congressional Fire Services Institute which is also associated with the folks you mention here. I know who these institutions are, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And now, I will not leave you in suspense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show 1D00182, which is a document authored by Varone from the internet, and I would direct the -- Madam Registrar to go to page 2 in e-court, and I'd like to focus on the fifth paragraph from the top of this document, and I'd like to present to you, sir, what Mr. Varone has written and then ask for your comment on the same. So please bear with me. And the part that I'm asking about starts off: "Lastly, once some fire-fighters in the community are known to be armed, the bad guys out there will likely assume that all fire-fighters in the community are armed. Admittedly, the argument can be made that that could work in our favour, but it may also serve to put unarmed fire-fighters at risk of pre-emptive attack. Most importantly, fire-fighters and EMS personnel may no longer be viewed by some in the community as the good guys but rather as armed agents of an oppressive government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Again, I would object to relevance. I don't see -- well, one, this appears to be a web page. If Mr. Ivetic could assist me as to how this was written by Mr. Patrone, that would be helpful. But, two, the relevance of domestic fire-fighters and whether or not an incident happens in Long [sic] Island and its relation to then the significance under US law and that -- how that would then relate in Sarajevo during war time, this article appears to have no relevance. We would add that also offering the opinions of an individual who is not testifying here is improper. The -- it should be based on what the witness knows and what his personal experiences are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may respond with the objections in the order that they came. The next page of the document indicates that this is posted by Curt Varone, not Patrone, Varone, the individual we discussed. This is his page. And it can be checked. That's the information that's there. I believe that this is relevant. We are talking about fire-fighting. We are talking about armed fire-fighters. And I am not presenting this for truth of the matter asserted, I am asking -- going to be asking Mr. Jordan to comment upon this and see if we can directly tie some of these concerns to the situation that Mr. Jordan saw in Sarajevo which is of direct relevance to us, and I believe it is in direct relevance to one Scheduled Incident of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber grants the objection not because the matter in itself could not be raised, but the way in which you do it. You introduce more or less expert opinion and then ask the witness to comment on it. Again, it's not a matter which could not be raised with the witness but not in this way. Mr. Jordan, have you considered when you decided to be armed, at least some members of your teams, what effect this would have on the population -- on the confidence of the population or armed forces would have in your functioning as fire-fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all due respect to Chief Varone, the casualties on the Sarajevo fire department from gun-fire and shelling exceeded 20 per cent of the department, one man in five, before we started addressing the issue of snipers. They -- they lost no one after we started protecting them to gun-fire at fires. That would be my answer to Mr. Varone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you were not asked to answer to Mr. Varone. You were asked to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was whether you have considered that at the time the effect as I described it, and as suggested as a possible --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Carefully considered it, sir, and talked to folks on both sides of the confrontation line before we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that when you say you considered the risk that there was considerable risk from proceeding armed in the course of performing fire-fighter duties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: With casualties standing at 20 per cent the first year into the war and with no end to the war in sight, I thought the risk of not actively protecting firemen would increase the risk to the fire department not existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at that time that you made this decision and accepted this risk, am I correct that there's not a single fire department or fire-fighter organisation which advocated that fire-fighters should be arrangement with military-grade 50 calibre sniper rifles and battle rifles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: My answer to that would that the BSA firemen were armed to the teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that your decision to proceed with the GOFRS personnel being armed was a result of your military background and military experiences, rather than your -- rather than what was taught to you in the basic fire-fighting course which you completed to train you as a fire-fighter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Looking at the casualties the firemen were taking and the best way to prevent them, the answer to that did lie in my military experience, but it was all to complete the fire-fighting job. We never got involved in anything that could be considered a force multiplier for either of the warring sides. We strictly protected firemen. So did not see what we were doing as even a combat operation. More like a constabulary-type thing. Whereas firemen traditionally do not carry arms, fire marshals in many countries do, and they address criminality involved with arson. Those men are allowed to arrest people who start fires or intend to start fires. Those firemen are armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, based upon your significant military experience and background and your training, would you agree with me that the standard rules of engagement used by many armed forces calls for an otherwise civilian personnel to become a legitimate target of deadly force if they are seen to be armed with a weapon and especially if they present offensive or defensive deadly fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: In most militaries, the person only has to be armed to be considered military. The uniform is a secondary issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And would you agree with me that GOFRS, or persons -- some of persons within GOFRS were not only armed but were presenting offensive deadly fire to persons that were armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I am not aware of anybody in GOFRS ever providing offensive fire. We only fired to defend unarmed firemen who were engaged by personnel who were armed and may or may not have been in uniform. We also only engaged to drive people off. We did not necessarily shoot to kill. We shoot to drive people off, because that is all it took in the vast majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can direct your attention to paragraph 24 of your statement. Here is where you state, and then I quote: "I would classify most of the shooters as marksmen, not snipers." Then later on you say: "Most of the shooting was with medium quality weapons with low-power scopes." Would you agree with me that here we're talking about the snipers that were shooting upon the GOFRS personnel in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I'm saying that I considered most of the people who were referred to as snipers as, in actuality, gunmen, not necessarily a trained sniper who could hit somebody a thousand yards away. The expression "sniper" in Sarajevo was used by just about anyone to refer to when anyone was shot when that was really not the case. Many of the people who were shot walking around were shot by men who fired a burst out of a window from a thousand yards away, and people would say the wounded person was hit by a sniper when they were actually hit by, you know, some guy literally holding a gun over a wall and letting a magazine go. They would say the person was shot by a sniper. If there were really that many good snipers there, there would have been more dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would the fact that these persons that were incorrectly referred to as snipers, would the fact that they were using low-power scopes, medium quality weapons, and were not persons with accuracy to be snipers, would that mean that they would have lower accuracy than someone who would be trained as a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit concerned and puzzled by "these persons." Did I understand, Mr. Jordan, your explanation well that you said, Not all of that shooting at long distance was the work of snipers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you say that nothing of it was done by trained snipers or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were snipers there but not in the numbers everybody talks about. If that was the case, I wouldn't be here. But there was a lot of random shooting by what I call gunmen. And in Sarajevo, every time somebody was shot they would say he was shot by a sniper but that just wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So do I understand your answer well that you say there have been snipers but not all of the fire which was attributed to snipers would have come from snipers because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that how I have understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how I'm saying it. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic. By the way, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Ivetic, if we would take a break of 20 minutes, there would be 20 minutes left in today's session. Would there be any way, first of all, I'll ask Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber, how much time do you think you would need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: About five minutes right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About five minutes. Let me check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would be able to conclude after the break in altogether 1 hour and 15 minutes rather than 1 hour and 20 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's doable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, then we could finish at quarter past 2.00. The Chamber may have a one or two questions. If that would be possible so that we try to conclude the evidence of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I indicated, it's doable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- today. Yes. Thank you. We'll take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 2.00. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I encourage, apart from that, for everyone to be here in time so that by a late start my bad reputation will not be further damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, prior to the break, we were talking about these marksmen, as you assessed them, that were not proper snipers with -- with -- with proper accuracy. Would you agree with me that your assessment included times when the GOFRS personnel were subjected to incoming fire. That is to say that sometimes the incoming fire upon the GOFRS came from such, as you called them, marksmen, rather than snipers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that there were times that civilians were struck by either sniper or marksmen fire while in the presence of members of the GOFRS, or near to members of the GOFRS, whether armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Because we would station ourselves in areas where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just ask that we break this up because I believe that the witness, at least in his own mind, has distinguished someone -- somewhat between what he considered to be a marksmen and what he considered to be a trained sniper. So if could we just break up, are we talking about what he considers to be the marksmen as opposed to trained snipers? As I believe [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- Mr. Ivetic please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, right now I'm only concerned about marksmen because that's what you're talking about. I believe that's how you're answering as well but --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Understood, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about marksmen, do you believe that there are times that civilians were struck by marksmen while nearby GOFRS personnel, irrespective of whether those GOFRS personnel were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you sit here today, you cannot exclude 100 per cent the possibility that the incident that we saw in the video-tape, the unfortunate incident with the mother and her child, was the result of a marksmen who missed one of the armed GOFRS men and struck those two unfortunate victims, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I can say with 100 per cent certainty that whoever shot the child could not see us at all because we would always station our vehicle under cover in front of the museum to where we were masked from any gun-fire and we would only break cover to assist casualties. So nobody took a shot at the kid -- nobody took a shot at us and hit the kid. Not a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, were the GOFRS personnel on scene armed on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Trevor Gibson would have had a 9-millimetre handgun on his hip and there may have been long guns in the vehicle, which in the video footage you will see none come out. It was not a situation where gun-fire by us would have been necessary. There was a Ukrainian APC and a French VAB there on site, which I believe shortly after did engage. So it was not a case where we would have to do it. We only did it when we have to, when there was no UNPROFOR to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question on this aspect before going into my last section. Have the occasions where GOFRS had fired upon, had -- they had taken out their weapons and fired, had those occurred prior to this incident? Had any of those occurred prior to this incident; that is to say, prior to this incident GOFRS had occasion to fire their weapons in, as you say, a defensive manner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to paragraph 23 of your statement, sir. Therein you state that the Bosnian Muslims had mobile mortars stored under cover and pulled out when they had to be used. Am I correct that such mortars could be placed anywhere in Sarajevo at short notice, even at civilian positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct these same mortars could be easily dismantled and hidden under cover again after being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as a -- based upon your military experience and training, and especially as a anti-tank specialist, is it standard procedure to try and triangulate and return fire upon a mortar position that has fired upon you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Counter-battery fire takes time, training, and talent. I didn't see a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you now answer my question, sir: Would it be standard operating procedure for an opposing party to try to triangulate and return fire upon a mortar position that had fired upon them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: In an organised, professional military establishment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to paragraph 35 of your statement, and just briefly, here, sir, you are telling us precisely about an incident when you eye-witness that the Bosnian Muslim forces used a portable motor to fire at Serb forces from the hospital building. Is this the same kind of mobile mortar that we were talking about in the prior paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it a...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of calibre and/or range these mobile mortars had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believe the one I saw fired that night was the 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the accuracy of such mortars? Would you accept the possibility that these mortars, fired in the manner that you saw them being fired by the Bosnian Muslim forces, could miss their targets and their shells could land elsewhere in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I described the fire as pointless and inaccurate in my statement, and I still hold to that now. Taking a mortar out and slapping it down on the ground and just firing around is just plain dumb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours. If you have a question, go ahead. I'm going to confer with my colleagues for just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could ask a clarifying question meanwhile. Do you consider it possible that such inaccurate firing an 82-millimetre mortar would result in the mortar landing within the territory of the force that fired it rather than at the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The term in military terms is short round. Short rounds occur more frequently than anybody would like. They occur when it is hastily set up. It occurs when there's a -- damage to the charges. All the powder may not go off and it could literally fall out the end of the tube. Mortars you have to know what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You -- in paragraph 35 you're talking about portable mortar fired from the hospital in late 1994. Which hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the -- the one in the compound. The Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Kosevo hospital. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Another area just to, I think, pull together all your experiences, sir, and a question that I skipped earlier.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that in addition to your own training as an anti-tank specialist that you also in the other wars that you say -- other combat situations that you saw prior to Bosnia, that you also had experience watching either friendly forces or opposing forces utilising such mobile mortars in combat in other situations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I've seen mortars used in combat. The anti-tank platoon, as in the heavy weapons platoon in the United States Military, the other complementary platoon is the mortar platoon, and any senior NCO winds up learning both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, I have completed you in the time period that the Judges have -- I quickly asked you questions within the time-period given to me. I thank you, sir, for coming here today and for your efforts to try and clarify your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I put on the record that you took even less time than was granted to you. Mr. Weber, if you're going to do the same, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before giving an opportunity, Judge Moloto would have one or more questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to be very quick, Mr. Jordan. Mr. Jordan, at page 65, lines 11 and 14 of the transcript, you were asked if on your first trip to Sarajevo you organised that personally and privately through the Bosnian Embassy. I was going to ask you, Bosnian Embassy to which country. However, at page 66, lines 7 and 9, you agreed with counsel for the Defence as to what you mean by Bosnian Embassy. I still don't understand what you mean by that. And there you said -- you said -- the question was: "And, sir, both you -- both and you and have I used the term Bosnian Embassy -- am I correct when you use that term you imply the forces that were applied with Mr. Izetbegovic?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I don't know what you mean by that. The normal understanding I have of the word "embassy" is an embassy is an embassy of a country in another country. Now Mr. Izetbegovic was a president. He couldn't be an ambassador. So I'm not quite sure what you mean here when you say forces -- forces that were applied with. You know, first of all, an embassy is not a force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, it's an office in another country representing its country. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I actually don't have the line you're talking about in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, page 66 -- unfortunately, it's badly recorded. Page 66, lines 7 to 9. It says: "And sir, both and you and have I used," you know. I suppose the intention was to say: Sir, both you and I have used the term "Bosnian Embassy," and am I correct when I say you use the term to imply the forces that were applied with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I mean "Bosnian embassy," I mean the BiH embassy; what was functioning as their embassy in the New York City at the time. That was my first meeting with the [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the question to my -- to the first question would have solved the question. Okay. It's the embassy in the US.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Weber, if you perform as well as Mr. Ivetic did, we will even be able to conclude the testimony of this witness by the end of today's session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, with respect to the members of GOFRS, were there volunteers who came from countries other than the United States?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What countries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We had folks from Canada, England, Scotland, Lebanon, France --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you lower your voice. No problem to consult with Mr. Lukic, but do it on a low voice. Please proceed, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Canada, England, Scotland, Lebanon, France, Spain, and one from the Czech Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At page 82, you stated: "Casualties on the Sarajevo fire department from gun-fire exceeded 20 per cent of the fire department." Were these Bosnian government fire-fighters armed when they were injured?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And did this, if I understand your testimony correctly, did this occur at a time prior to when you or any other members of GOFRS even carried any arms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think that's what the witness told us already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We only took arms once. So therefore there was no need to put that question again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, you describe an occasion in July 1995 which you were asked about where you suspect the mortar fire coming from the Bosnian Muslim side. Were there any other occasions besides this one incident in July 1995 that you believe Bosnian Muslim forces fired upon you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Only one occasion. Some desultory small arms fire, but no heavy weapons fire. The violence in and around Sarajevo was basically shoveled downhill and spooned uphill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I mean, there are a lot less guns in the city than there were around the city so -- and the confrontation lines really weren't going to change, so ... it was just a question of where all the guns were and there were more around the town than in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And who were the ones around the town that were using or in your analogy shovelling downhill?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Well, that would be the BSA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Going back to that same paragraph where you discuss the mobile mortars, and counsel also brought up the incident in late 1994 in paragraph 35 where you saw it at the Kosevo hospital. Were there any other occasions that you saw the mobile mortars besides that occasion at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No, it was just that one occasion that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How often did you go to this hospital, the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We -- in the course of moving all about town responding to shootings and shellings and some ordinary medical evacuations we would be just about any place in town on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I briefly apologise. I have been asked to convey a request from Mr. Mladic that he wished to address two specific questions to this witness himself personally. I don't know if this -- if Your Honours are open to doing that. I'm conveying the request on behalf of Mr. Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not allowed to put questions himself to this witness, but if there are any questions he would convey to you, then, of course, we will consider whether we grant you a couple of minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. I might be able to assist if I can go closer to Mr. Mladic to try to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And switch your microphones off and lower the voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Mladic again has asked me to convey that he has approximately 30 words that he would like to read out for Your Honours, and it has to do with the accuracy of so-called smart technology weapons as opposed to the conventional weapons that were used in Sarajevo. I'm at your disposal, obviously, for -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not allowed to read out such a statement at this moment. Of course, you know exactly if it's a relevant matter how counsel can address the Chamber on these matters, either through filings or through cross-examination of future witnesses or, if it ever comes to that stage, in the presentation of your own case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have advised him so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, if there's a question that Mr. Mladic would like to put to the witness, he can put it through you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before that we would give you a couple of minutes for that. Then this ... Mr. Jordan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'd like to continue with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, this then concludes your evidence. May I take it, Mr. Ivetic, that you had no questions for yourself. You had no questions you had on your list apart from [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I did not have any further questions for the witness. I'd already excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for 30 seconds to see whether there is any specific question you'd like to put on behalf of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Jordan, if there are no questions, and we have to wait for 30 seconds to know that, I already would like to thank you very much for having coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions, perhaps minus one, that were put by the parties and by the Bench, and I already waiting for the outcome of this consultation. I would already wish you a safe return home anyhow today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any further question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Then the witness is excused and may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn -- we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 29th of August, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of August, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
